key_insight: Machine-learned dynamics shows that small polarons on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move far more slowly than in bulk because surface geometry removes favorable hopping routes and confines motion to limited pathways.
engineering_relevance: This explains why porous rutile TiO2 can have much lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, informing design of oxide surfaces for catalysis, photovoltaics, batteries, and energy storage.
method: Extended a machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics framework to a reducible oxide surface.
Ran nanosecond-scale finite-temperature simulations on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110).
Compared surface polaron hopping behavior with bulk-like transport pathways.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports several nanoseconds of dynamics across multiple temperatures, showing a several-orders-of-magnitude suppression of surface polaron mobility relative to bulk.
watch_item: The conclusions are system-specific to reduced rutile TiO2(110), so transfer to other oxides or defect densities should be validated before reuse.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
